prompt: Explain the federal budget using only football metaphors. Do not stop when they stop working.
response:
Alright, let’s break down the Team USA front office playbook. Put on your helmet, because we are going deep into the Xs and Os of the ultimate franchise salary cap: the Federal Budget.

**The Salary Cap and Revenue (Taxes)**
Every season begins with the front office looking at how much cash the season ticket holders (the citizens) are bringing into the stadium. You’ve got your general admission ticket sales (income tax), your luxury box corporate sponsorships (corporate taxes), and the mandatory stadium facility fees everyone pays at the gate (payroll taxes). This is the team’s total available cap space. 

**Guaranteed Veteran Contracts (Mandatory Spending)**
Before the Head Coach (the President) and the Offensive Coordinators (Congress) can even draw up a single play, they have to pay out the guaranteed veteran contracts. These are deals negotiated decades ago that cannot be cut without a massive dead-cap penalty and an offseason locker room revolt. This is your Social Security and Medicare—basically, the lifetime pensions for all the Hall of Famers and the medical bills for players on permanent Injured Reserve. Over 60% of our entire salary cap is eaten up by these un-cuttable veteran deals before the draft even starts. 

**The Weekly Game Plan (Discretionary Spending)**
Whatever cap space is left over is used for the weekly game plan. Half of this remaining money goes straight to the middle linebackers and the pass rush—that’s the Defense Department. We pay top dollar for the biggest, hardest-hitting defensive line in the league so nobody tries a Hail Mary into our endzone. 

The rest of the discretionary cap space goes to the offensive line, special teams, and stadium maintenance. This goes toward paying the scouting department (scientific research), patching up the turf (infrastructure), and making sure the rookie development squad has enough Gatorade (education).

**Void Years and Borrowing (The Deficit)**
Here’s where the playbook gets wild. The season ticket holders don’t actually buy enough tickets to cover the roster we’ve built. So, every single season, the General Manager restructures the deals by adding "void years." This means we are signing free agents today, but deferring their signing bonuses to the 2045 salary cap. When we spend more cap space in a single season than the stadium actually brought in, that gap is the Deficit. We are basically trading our future first-round draft picks to other teams (and sometimes to our own fans) for cash considerations today.
